1. Read the CSV (or equivalent) containing the 33-row table of borough names and the two crime-rate columns (“second_half_2010_value”, “first_half_2011_value”).  
2. Remove any borough that has a missing value in EITHER of the two columns (because a change cannot be computed without both numbers).  This yields a clean data set on which all subsequent calculations are done.  
3. Compute the change for each remaining borough: Δ = first_half_2011_value − second_half_2010_value.  Keep this as a 1-D NumPy array z.  
4. Build the binary neighbour adjacency matrix W (33 × 33 before any rows are dropped) from the provided neighbour lists:  
   • wᵢⱼ = 1 if borough j is listed as a geographic neighbour of borough i, else 0.  
   • Set the diagonal to 0.  
   • After dropping any boroughs in Step 2, synchronously drop the corresponding rows and columns from W so that its dimensions match the length of z.  
5. Row-standardise the weight matrix: divide each row of W by its row sum so that every non-isolated row sums to 1. (If a borough has no neighbours after cleaning—which is unlikely—drop it as well.)  
6. Compute Global Moran’s I for the change vector z with the row-standardised W:

      I = (N / ΣₖΣₗ wₖₗ) · (ΣₖΣₗ wₖₗ (zₖ − ȳ)(zₗ − ȳ)) / Σₖ (zₖ − ȳ)²,

   where N is the number of boroughs after cleaning and ȳ is the mean of z.  
7. Assess statistical significance by a Monte-Carlo permutation test:  
   a. Randomly permute z 999 times (≥ 500 as required).  
   b. For each permutation, recompute Moran’s I, storing the null distribution.  
   c. The two-sided p-value = (count of |I_perm| ≥ |I_obs| + 1) / (999 + 1).  
8. Interpretation rule:  
   • If p < 0.05 and I_obs > 0 ⇒ changes are positively spatially clustered (neighbouring boroughs tend to show changes in the same direction).  
   • If p < 0.05 and I_obs < 0 ⇒ changes are spatially dispersed (neighbours tend to change in opposite directions).  
   • Otherwise (p ≥ 0.05) ⇒ no evidence of spatial autocorrelation in the change.  
9. Report the observed Moran’s I and the p-value, rounded to 3–4 decimals, and decide between “CLUSTERED” or “NOT CLUSTERED” following the rule in Step 8.  
10. Print the conclusion exactly in the required format:

     FINAL ANSWER: CLUSTERED (test statistic = <I_obs>, p = <p_val>)
     or
     FINAL ANSWER: NOT CLUSTERED (test statistic = <I_obs>, p = <p_val>)

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# -----------------------------
# 1. Load the two supplied CSVs
# -----------------------------
DATA_PATH = "chunks_csv/changespillover/changespillover_no2crime_crime_second_half_2010_to_first_half_2011.csv"
ADJ_PATH  = "chunks_csv/borough_adjacency.csv"

df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH)
adj = pd.read_csv(ADJ_PATH)

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 2. Drop any borough with a missing value in either period
# ----------------------------------------------------
df_clean = df.dropna(subset=["second_half_2010_value", "first_half_2011_value"]).copy()
df_clean["change"] = df_clean["first_half_2011_value"] - df_clean["second_half_2010_value"]

# Keep only the borough names we still have
boroughs = df_clean["borough"].tolist()
N = len(boroughs)

# -----------------------------------------
# 3. Build an undirected adjacency matrix W
# -----------------------------------------
# Filter adjacency list so that both borough and neighbour are in the cleaned set
adj_filtered = adj[adj["borough"].isin(boroughs) & adj["neighbor"].isin(boroughs)].copy()

# Map borough names to indices
idx = {b: i for i, b in enumerate(boroughs)}

# Initialise matrix
W = np.zeros((N, N), dtype=float)

# Fill symmetric adjacency
for _, row in adj_filtered.iterrows():
    i = idx[row["borough"]]
    j = idx[row["neighbor"]]
    W[i, j] = 1
    W[j, i] = 1   # ensure undirected

# Remove any potential isolates (rows with all zeros)
row_sums = W.sum(axis=1)
if (row_sums == 0).any():
    keep_mask = row_sums > 0
    # Update data structures synchronously
    W = W[keep_mask][:, keep_mask]
    df_clean = df_clean.loc[keep_mask].reset_index(drop=True)
    boroughs = df_clean["borough"].tolist()
    N = len(boroughs)

# Re-compute row_sums after any removals
row_sums = W.sum(axis=1)

# Row-standardise so each non-isolated row sums to 1
W = W / row_sums[:, None]

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 4. Compute observed Global Moran’s I for the change
# ---------------------------------------------------
z = df_clean["change"].to_numpy(float)
z_bar = z.mean()
z_centered = z - z_bar

# Denominator
S0 = W.sum()            # After row-standardisation this equals N
numerator = (z_centered @ W @ z_centered)
denominator = (z_centered ** 2).sum()
I_obs = (N / S0) * (numerator / denominator)    # equivalent to numerator/denominator because S0=N

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Permutation test (999 random shuffles => 1000 totals)
# ----------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=0)
n_perm = 999
I_perm = np.empty(n_perm)

for k in range(n_perm):
    z_perm = rng.permutation(z_centered)
    I_perm[k] = (N / S0) * ((z_perm @ W @ z_perm) / denominator)

# Two-sided p-value with +1 correction (Anselin 1995)
p_val = (np.sum(np.abs(I_perm) >= abs(I_obs)) + 1) / (n_perm + 1)

# Decide verdict
verdict = "CLUSTERED" if p_val < 0.05 else "NOT CLUSTERED"

# ---------------------------
# 6. Print required sentences
# ---------------------------
print(f"data_points_used = {N}")
print(f"FINAL ANSWER: {verdict} (Moran_I = {I_obs:.4f}, p = {p_val:.4f})")
